latin.225: Secunda, Hoc potest illustrari & confirmari promissione & comminatione foederis legalis. Pollicebatur vitam, hoc fac & vives. Quam? spiritualem illam positam in justitia & sanctitate? nihil minus: eius nec initium, nec progressum, nec continuationem lex promittebat, sed exigebat. Promissiones foederis legalis erant conditionales. Conditio erat perfecta justitia perpetuo conservata. Sub hac conditione promittebatur vita. Quare vita promissa non potuit sita esse in praesentia justitiae. Iam autem mors, quam lex comminabatur, opposita erat formaliter non conditioni, sed vitae promissae: non consistebat igitur in absentia seu privatione justitiae.
latin.226: PLAC. Hanc secundam rationem D. Garissolius alto Silentio praeteriit.
latin.227: Tertia, violatio conditionis sive praecepti non est poena transgressori denunciata. Sed privatio justitiae est violatio conditionis seu praecepti. Ergo non est poena transgressori denunciata. Major probatione non eget: Minorem sic demonstro. Quod lex prohibet, id legis violatio est. At lex prohibet absentiam justitiae in homine (tam certe quam jubet homini justitiam inesse.) Ergo absentia justitiae (quae tibi mors est spiritualis) violatio est legis.
latin.228: GAR. Respond. De majore litem hic non moveo: disputabitur inferius, an violatio praecepti divini, quae peccatum est, possit esse poena peccati. Ad minorem dico, distinguendam esse privationem justitiae, ut aliam activam nominemus, aliam passivam. Activa est, qua homo ipse male agendo justitia seipsum spoliat, qua Deus illum impertiverat: passiva qua Deus hominem justitia privat, & donis quibus ipsum cumularat. Si ergo agnoscimus privationem activam justitiae idem esse cum violatione legis; de privatione tamen passiva id merito negabitur.
latin.229: PLAC. Quod de majore litem hic non movet, prudenter facit: nam praeter tres illas rationes, quae sequuntur in Manuscripto, ad quas nihil respondit, violatio conditionis seu praecepti prima nec antecedentis peccati poena esse potest, cum sit peccatum primum, nec sui ipsius, cum non possit posterior esse seipsa: & ridicule apponeretur praecepto comminatio, quae minaretur fore ut violetur praeceptum, si violetur. Minorem argumento confirmaveram, quod illi visum est tutius silentio tegere, quam attingere. Potest etiam sic probari. Peccatum est violatio legis. Privatio justitiae in homine, est peccatum. Ergo privatio justitiae est violatio legis. Quid clarius? At ille distinguit privationem justitiae in activam & passivam: illam qua homo ipse male agendo justitia seipsum spoliat, hanc qua Deus hominem justitia privat: illam fatetur esse violationem legis, hanc negat. Ex quo sequitur, hanc, non illam, legem esse suo violatori comminatam. Consideremus igitur paulo attentius illam distinctionem. Recte sane privatio justitiae activa dicitur respectu privantis se justitia hominis: activa enim dicitur respectu agentis. Sed passiva, cur non similiter dicitur respectu privati seu patientis hominis? Nam ut privans respondet privato, agens patienti, actio passioni, ita videtur privatio active sumpta esse privantis, passive vero privati? Cur ergo passiva tribuitur Deo, qui privat hominem justitia, non privatur ullo modo? Hoc primum.
latin.230: Deinde si se homo ipse privat justitia, nonne hoc satis est ut sit justitia privatus? Quid opus est, ut postquam sese ipse privavit justitia, Deus eum privet justitia? oportet enim hanc privationem illa posteriorem esse, siquidem illa est violatio legis, haec illam violationem consequens poena. Praeterea, quaero, privatio justitiae originalis quatenus fuit in Adamo, aut est in nobis omnibus, qualis sit privatio? si est activa, habeo quod volo, est violatio legis, non autem poena lege denunciata. Si est passiva, non est violatio legis, non est peccatum, sed poena tantum. Id quod est negare peccatum originale. Denique, Docet-ne alicubi Scriptura Deum privasse Adamum justitia? Quomodo ergo ausus est Vir Doctus id asserere? Certe, qua ducor erga Deum reverentia, ferre non potest mea conscientia illam assertionem. Nam qui privat hominem justitia, facit eum injustum ejusque injustitiae causa est. Id quod vel suspicari de Deo mihi nefas esse videtur. Sed secundam affert Vir Doctus responsionem, qua tollit id quod dedit: eam audiamus.
latin.231: GAR. 2. Si rem diligenter attendimus, patebit privationem activam justitiae, qua scil. homo amittit justitiam & ea seipsum spoliat, non esse formaliter idem cum violatione praecepti divini. Itaque verum quidem erit in sensu causali violationem divini praecepti esse justitiae privationem, quia scilicet ex violatione consequitur illa privatio; quo sensu dicitur dolor esse solutio continui, quia ad solutionem continui sequitur: sed in sensu formali non erit verum, ita scilicet ut reapse unum idemque sint, nec differant, nisi nominibus. PLAC. Ego vero existimo, privationem pro distinctione termini seu formae, cujus est privatio, distingui debere. Est autem justitia duplex, actualis nempe, & habitualis. Forma mali moralis, seu peccati collocari solet in privatione boni. Justitiae igitur actualis privatio est formaliter peccatum actuale; justitiae vero habitualis privatio est formaliter malum seu peccatum habituale. Nonne? Cum ergo actualis violatio legis formaliter opponatur justitiae actuali, hoc est, inobedientia obedientiae, necesse est ut actualis violatio legis sit formaliter actualis privatio justitiae, & cum habitualis violatio legis seu inobedientia formaliter opponatur habituali justitiae seu obedientiae, necesse est ut ipsa quoque sit formaliter privatio justitiae habitualis, atque adeo peccatum habituale. Sed contra disputat Vir Doctus tribus rationibus.

pass_a.225: Second, This can be illustrated and confirmed by the promise and threat of the legal covenant. Life was promised, do this and you will live. What life? that spiritual one placed in justice and holiness? nothing less: the law promised neither its beginning nor progress nor continuation, but demanded them. The promises of the legal covenant were conditional. The condition was perfect justice perpetually preserved. Under this condition life was promised. Therefore the promised life could not be situated in the presence of justice. But now the death which the law threatened was formally opposed not to the condition but to the promised life: therefore it did not consist in the absence or privation of justice.
pass_a.226: PLAC. This second reason D. Garissolius passed over in deep silence.
pass_a.227: Third, violation of the condition or precept is not a penalty denounced to the transgressor. But privation of justice is violation of the condition or precept. Therefore it is not a penalty denounced to the transgressor. The major needs no proof: the minor I demonstrate thus. What the law forbids is a violation of the law. But the law forbids absence of justice in a man (as certainly as it commands justice to be in a man). Therefore absence of justice (which for you is spiritual death) is a violation of the law.
pass_a.228: GAR. Reply. About the major I raise no dispute here: it will be disputed below whether violation of a divine precept, which is sin, can be the penalty of sin. To the minor I say that privation of justice must be distinguished, so that we name one active, another passive. Active is that by which the man himself by acting badly strips himself of the justice with which God had endowed him: passive that by which God deprives the man of justice and of the gifts with which he had heaped him. If therefore we acknowledge that active privation of justice is the same as violation of the law, yet of passive privation that will deservedly be denied.
pass_a.229: PLAC. That he does not move a dispute about the major here he does prudently: for besides those three reasons which follow in the Manuscript, to which he answered nothing, violation of the condition or precept first cannot be the penalty of an antecedent sin, since it is the first sin, nor of itself, since it cannot be later than itself: and ridiculously would a threat be attached to a precept which threatened that the precept would be violated if it were violated. The minor I had confirmed by an argument which it seemed safer to him to cover with silence than to touch. It can also be proved thus. Sin is violation of the law. Privation of justice in a man is sin. Therefore privation of justice is violation of the law. What clearer? But he distinguishes privation of justice into active and passive: that by which the man himself by acting badly strips himself of justice, this by which God deprives the man of justice: that he confesses to be violation of the law, this he denies. From which it follows that this, not that, was the law threatened to its violator. Let us therefore consider that distinction a little more attentively. Rightly indeed privation of justice is called active with respect to the man privating himself of justice: for active is said with respect to the agent. But passive — why is it not similarly said with respect to the privated or patient man? For as the privating answers to the privated, agent to patient, action to passion, so active privation seems to be of the privating, passive truly of the privated? Why then is the passive attributed to God, who deprives the man of justice, is not himself privated in any way? This first.
pass_a.230: Next, if the man himself privates himself of justice, is this not enough that he be privated of justice? What need is there that after he has privated himself of justice God should deprive him of justice? for this privation must be later than that, if that is violation of the law, this the consequent penalty of that violation. Further I ask, privation of original justice as it was in Adam or is in us all — of what sort is the privation? if active, I have what I want: it is violation of the law, not however a penalty denounced by the law. If passive, it is not violation of the law, not sin, but only penalty. Which is to deny original sin. Finally, does Scripture anywhere teach that God privated Adam of justice? How then did the Learned Man dare to assert it? Certainly the reverence by which I am led toward God cannot let my conscience bear that assertion. For who privates a man of justice makes him unjust and is the cause of his injustice. Which even to suspect of God seems to me unlawful. But the Learned Man brings a second reply by which he takes away what he gave: let us hear it.
pass_a.231: GAR. 2. If we attend the matter carefully, it will appear that active privation of justice, by which namely a man loses justice and strips himself of it, is not formally the same as violation of the divine precept. And so it will indeed be true in a causal sense that violation of the divine precept is privation of justice, because namely from the violation that privation follows; in which sense pain is called a solution of the continuum, because it follows upon solution of the continuum: but in a formal sense it will not be true, namely so that in the thing itself they are one and the same and differ only in names. PLAC. But I judge that privation ought to be distinguished according to the distinction of the term or form of which it is the privation. Now justice is twofold, actual namely and habitual. The form of moral evil or of sin is usually placed in the privation of a good. Therefore privation of actual justice is formally actual sin; but privation of habitual justice is formally habitual evil or sin. Is it not so? Since therefore actual violation of the law is formally opposed to actual justice, that is, disobedience to obedience, it is necessary that actual violation of the law be formally actual privation of justice, and since habitual violation of the law or disobedience is formally opposed to habitual justice or obedience, it is necessary that it also be formally privation of habitual justice, and so habitual sin. But against this the Learned Man disputes with three reasons.

225: Second proof. The legal covenant's own promise and threat make the same point. Life was pledged under the formula "do this and you will live." Was that the spiritual life grounded in righteousness and holiness? Far from it. The law never promised the start, growth, or continuance of that life; it demanded them. Legal-covenant promises were conditional, and the condition was perfect righteousness kept without break. Life was promised only under that condition—so the thing promised cannot have been identical with righteousness itself already present. And the death the law threatened stood formally over against the promised life, not against the condition. Hence that death was not the absence or stripping-away of righteousness.
226: Placeus. Garissoles met this second argument with total silence.
227: Third proof: breaking the condition or precept is not itself the penalty announced against the breaker. But loss of righteousness is breaking the condition or precept. Therefore that loss is not the announced penalty. The major is obvious; I prove the minor as follows. Whatever the law forbids is a breach of the law. The law forbids righteousness being absent from a man as firmly as it commands righteousness to be in him. Therefore that absence—which you call spiritual death—is a breach of the law.
228: Garissoles replies. I will not contest the major here; later we can ask whether breaking a divine precept (which is sin) can also be sin's penalty. On the minor I distinguish two privations of righteousness: active and passive. Active is the man's own bad acting by which he strips himself of the righteousness God had given him. Passive is God's stripping the man of that righteousness and of the gifts heaped on him. Grant that the active privation is the same as law-breaking; the passive still is not.
229: Placeus. He is wise not to fight the major here. Besides three further Manuscript reasons he never answered, the first breach of the condition cannot be the penalty of some earlier sin—because it is the first sin—nor the penalty of itself, since nothing is later than itself. It would be absurd to attach to a precept a threat that the precept will be broken if it is broken. I had already confirmed the minor by an argument he preferred to bury in silence rather than face. Another proof: sin is law-breaking; privation of righteousness in a man is sin; therefore that privation is law-breaking. Clearer still? Yet he splits privation into active and passive—the man's self-stripping versus God's stripping—and admits only the first as law-breaking. So on his view the threatened law-penalty is the second, not the first. Look harder at that split. "Active" rightly names privation from the agent's side—the man who strips himself. Why then is "passive" not named from the patient's side—the man stripped? Privating answers to privated, agent to patient, action to passion; so active privation belongs to the one who strips, passive to the one stripped. How then is the "passive" assigned to God, who strips the man and is never himself stripped? That is the first point.
230: Second: if the man has already stripped himself of righteousness, is that not enough for him to be without it? Why must God strip him again afterward? The divine stripping would have to come later than the self-stripping, if the latter is the law-breach and the former its following penalty. Third I ask what sort of privation original righteousness is, in Adam and in us. If active, I win: it is law-breaking, not a legally announced penalty. If only passive, it is neither law-breaking nor sin but bare penalty—and that denies original sin. Fourth: does any Scripture say God stripped Adam of righteousness? How then dare the learned man assert it? Reverence for God will not let my conscience bear that claim. Whoever strips a man of righteousness makes him unjust and causes his injustice—an idea I may not even entertain of God. But now he offers a second reply that retracts what he just gave; let us hear it.
231: Garissoles' second reply. Attend carefully and active privation of righteousness—losing it and stripping oneself of it—is not formally identical with breaking the divine precept. Causally one may say precept-breaking is privation of righteousness, because the privation follows the breach (as pain is called a dissolving of continuity because it follows that dissolving). Formally they are not one thing under two names.

Placeus. I take privation to track the form of which it is the privation. Righteousness itself is twofold: actual and habitual. Moral evil, or sin, is usually formalized as privation of a good. So privation of actual righteousness is formally actual sin, and privation of habitual righteousness is formally habitual evil or sin. Is that not so? Actual law-breaking stands formally opposite actual righteousness—disobedience opposite obedience—so actual law-breaking is formally actual privation of righteousness. Likewise habitual disobedience stands formally opposite habitual righteousness, so it too is formally privation of habitual righteousness, that is, habitual sin. Against this the learned man brings three arguments.
